name: FeynmanModel
summary: Represents a model of particles and Feynman-rule vertices read from CalcHEP model tables.

syntaxes.description: stores the four model tables used by the Feynman backend.

details: A [FeynmanModel](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanModel) is the model object to use when you want HEPCAT to calculate a tree amplitude from ordinary Feynman rules. Read a model with [ReadModel](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ReadModel), keep the returned object in a variable, and pass it to [CreateDiagrams](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/CreateDiagrams). The usual diagram workflow then produces Dirac and Lorentz tensors for that model.

The four arguments are, in order, the particle table, vertex table, independent parameter table and dependent function table. You can inspect them with `model[[1]]` through `model[[4]]`. Normally you obtain these tables from the model reader rather than assembling the object yourself.

The explicit head distinguishes a Feynman-rule model from a constructive model containing known amplitudes. [ReadModel](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ReadModel) selects the appropriate representation from the files in the model directory. A directory containing `lgrngN.mdl` supplies Feynman rules; a constructive `ampsN.mdl` file supplies on-shell amplitudes.

examples.description: Read the bundled massive-electron QED Feynman model.
Inspect the four tables without changing the model.

detail_sections.title: Using the model in a calculation
paragraphs: Generate the diagrams, obtain their amplitudes, and use [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) to express the result in HEPCAT spinor notation. [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes) can perform conversion and ordinary reduction together when given the Feynman model.

Parameters are kept in the model as [ModelParameter](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ModelParameter) objects. Loading a second model therefore does not replace the masses and couplings of the first. Use [ModelParameterRules](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ModelParameterRules) when you need the numerical values belonging to one particular model.

detail_sections.title: Scope of the Feynman calculation
paragraphs: Internal Feynman propagators and their numerator momenta remain off shell. External wavefunctions obey the external-particle conventions of HEPCAT. Keeping this distinction makes the result useful as an independent comparison with a constructive amplitude.

The supported physical tree backend uses unitary-gauge massive-vector propagators and excludes Goldstone and ghost exchange consistently. Model interactions and particle data still come from the supplied CalcHEP tables. Unsupported Majorana flow or higher-spin fields return `Failure`.

For a factorization check, supply a constructive model containing complete lower-point amplitudes to [FactorizationAmplitudeChannels](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FactorizationAmplitudeChannels). A table of Feynman vertices describes the interactions, and is not itself a table of those complete amplitudes.

name: DiracWord
summary: Keeps the order of gamma matrices and momentum slashes along a fermion line.

syntaxes.description: represents an ordered product of Dirac matrices and slashed momenta.

details: Use `DiracWord` inside a [DiracChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracChain) to write the operators between its two external fermions. Matrix multiplication is ordered: the first operator is next to the left endpoint, and the last is next to the right endpoint.

The operators accepted by [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) are [DiracGamma](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracGamma), [DiracGamma5](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracGamma5), [DiracSlash](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracSlash) and the identity `1`. `DiracWord[]` is the identity operator and is useful for a scalar fermion coupling.

A `DiracWord` is a symbolic record of an ordered matrix product. Ordinary Mathematica multiplication with `Times` does not represent that ordering. Put scalar coupling factors outside the word, and use separate terms for a sum of matrix products.

HEPCAT normally creates these words when it builds Feynman diagrams. You can inspect a word to follow the momentum insertions in a numerator, then convert the complete contracted expression with [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts).

examples.description: Record a momentum slash between two gamma matrices. The operator order follows the fermion line from left to right.

name: DiracGamma
summary: Represents a gamma matrix with a Lorentz index in an ordered fermion-line numerator.

syntaxes.description: represents a Dirac gamma matrix carrying a Lorentz index.

details: `DiracGamma[mu]` denotes the matrix carrying the Lorentz index `mu`. Place it in a [DiracWord](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracWord) to specify where it acts along a fermion line.

The index is a contraction label, not a numerical matrix component. For example, a current containing `DiracGamma[mu]` can contract with another current or with [LorentzMomentum](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzMomentum). The same index must occur twice in each term passed to [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts).
Changing the order of gamma matrices changes the numerator. An interchange requires the Clifford identity; it cannot be performed by sorting the arguments of a word.

For a momentum-contracted gamma matrix, [DiracSlash](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracSlash) is often the clearer representation. Conversion uses HEPCAT's Weyl and external-state conventions, so relative signs follow the same conventions as the resulting [SpinorChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/SpinorChain) expressions.

examples.description: Write two gamma matrices with their order explicit. The Lorentz labels can later be contracted with the rest of a diagram.

name: DiracGamma5
summary: Represents the chirality matrix acting at a specified position in a Dirac word.

syntaxes.description: represents the chirality matrix in an ordered Dirac word.

details: `DiracGamma5` is a symbol used as an operator inside [DiracWord](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracWord). It does not take a Lorentz index. Its position records which matrices lie to its left and right.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) uses `gamma5 = diag(-1,+1)` in its Weyl-block convention. This determines the signs of the angle and square contributions to a chiral coupling.

Chiral projectors are linear combinations of the identity and this matrix. Keep the corresponding scalar coefficients and separate matrix terms when representing a projector explicitly. `DiracWord[]` supplies the identity part.

The model reader inserts chirality operators from the supplied vertex rules. For routine model calculations, let [ReadModel](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ReadModel) and the diagram code retain these operators until conversion, rather than adding helicity signs by hand.

examples.description: Keep gamma5 on the right of the vector vertex, where its chirality sign is applied during conversion.

name: DiracSlash
summary: Represents a four-momentum contracted with gamma matrices inside a Dirac word.

syntaxes.description: represents a momentum contracted with a Dirac gamma matrix.

details: `DiracSlash[Mom[k]]` denotes the slash of momentum `k`. Its position in a [DiracWord](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracWord) matters just as the position of a gamma matrix does.

The momentum can be a single [Mom](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/Mom) object, a sum of such objects, or a [Multiparticle](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/Multiparticle) momentum. For example, `DiracSlash[Mom[Multiparticle[1,3]]]` records the numerator momentum of an internal line carrying `p1+p3`.

During [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts), the slash becomes a momentum insertion in the resulting [SpinorChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/SpinorChain). An internal momentum remains off shell, even if the associated propagator has a known mass.

External Dirac identities can reduce an insertion when it acts next to the corresponding external spinor. This external reduction does not justify replacing the square of an internal slash by its propagator mass.

examples.description: Keep the internal momentum p1+p3 as one slash in the numerator. Its square is not assumed to equal an internal mass.

name: LorentzIndex
summary: Labels a Lorentz index in a Feynman vertex or diagram expression.

syntaxes.description: labels a Lorentz slot in a Feynman tensor.

details: `LorentzIndex[slot]` names a Lorentz slot of a vertex. You will see it in parsed rules containing [LorentzMetric](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzMetric), [LorentzMomentum](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzMomentum) or [DiracGamma](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracGamma). Diagram generation attaches these local vertex slots to the incident lines.
`LorentzIndex[slot,2]` names a second slot of a tensor auxiliary field. The second argument distinguishes two indices carried by the same field; it does not refer to a second external particle.

For a complete scalar amplitude, every Lorentz contraction label must occur exactly twice in each term. [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) checks this condition. A free index usually means that the supplied expression is still a current or tensor, rather than a complete amplitude.
You normally inspect these labels while following a raw diagram. There is no need to assign them values or sum numerical components by hand.

examples.description: Name the two metric slots of a local Feynman vertex.

name: LorentzMetric
summary: Represents the Minkowski metric used to contract Lorentz indices in a Feynman expression.

syntaxes.description: represents the Minkowski metric with two Lorentz indices.

details: `LorentzMetric[mu,nu]` represents the metric with signature `(+,-,-,-)`. Its two arguments label the tensor indices to be contracted.

For example, the product `LorentzMetric[mu,nu] LorentzMomentum[Mom[1],mu] LorentzMomentum[Mom[2],nu]` represents the scalar product of two momenta. [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) contracts such products before writing the answer with [MomProd](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/MomProd) and spinor chains.

A single metric with different free indices is a tensor, not a scalar amplitude. Conversion of a complete amplitude requires all its indices to be contracted. A repeated metric index represents the four-dimensional trace.

Use [LorentzScalarProduct](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzScalarProduct) for a dot product that is already contracted and [LorentzMomentum](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzMomentum) for a momentum with one index still exposed.

examples.description: Write the metric acting on a momentum. The remaining free index makes this a vector tensor, ready for another contraction.
Contract the four-dimensional metric trace. This is a scalar expression with no external wavefunctions.

name: LorentzMomentum
summary: Represents a momentum with one Lorentz index available for contraction.

syntaxes.description: represents a four-momentum carrying a Lorentz index.

details: `LorentzMomentum[p,mu]` is the `mu` component of a symbolic momentum. Use a [Mom](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/Mom) object or supported linear combination for `p`; `mu` is a contraction label.

Two factors carrying the same index, such as `LorentzMomentum[Mom[3],mu] LorentzMomentum[Mom[4],mu]`, form a scalar product. A contraction with [DiracGamma](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracGamma) instead supplies a slash in the fermion numerator.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) performs these contractions in a complete Feynman expression. It expands supported momentum sums as needed while retaining the off-shell values of internal momentum squares.

This head is useful while reading a Feynman tensor expression. After conversion, the corresponding information is represented by [MomProd](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/MomProd) or momentum insertions in [SpinorChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/SpinorChain).

examples.description: Represent the contracted product p3.p4 before spinor conversion.
Convert the contracted momentum factors. The result is a HEPCAT scalar product that can be used with the spinor algebra.

name: LorentzScalarProduct
summary: Represents a contracted momentum dot product before Feynman-rule conversion.

syntaxes.description: retains an off-shell scalar product in a Feynman rule.

details: `LorentzScalarProduct[p,q]` records `p.q` in a Feynman vertex. Unlike [LorentzMomentum](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/LorentzMomentum), it has no exposed Lorentz index: the contraction is already specified.

Its arguments can contain sums of [Mom](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/Mom) objects. The reader keeps this form while the momenta still refer to local vertex slots. Diagram generation then attaches those slots to actual diagram momenta.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) distributes the scalar product over the supported momentum sums and writes the result with [MomProd](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/MomProd). Internal momenta remain off shell throughout this conversion.
The presence of an internal mass in a propagator does not set this scalar product to that mass squared. The retained virtuality is part of the ordinary Feynman numerator.

examples.description: Keep a dot product with the composite momentum p1+p3 visible before conversion distributes it.
Distribute a dot product over its momentum sum while keeping every momentum off shell.

name: FermionBar
summary: Records the left antifermion wavefunction of an all-incoming Dirac chain.

syntaxes.description: represents the left antifermion endpoint of an ordered Dirac chain.

details: `FermionBar[leg,mass,chirality]` is the left endpoint of a [DiracChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracChain). The first argument identifies the external momentum, and the second supplies that particle's mass.

The usual massive Dirac endpoint has chirality tag `"Dirac"`. Model-defined chiral fields use `"L"` or `"R"`. The tag selects the field components; it is not a choice of spin state for a massive fermion.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) uses the all-incoming antifermion convention `bar v = (<p|,-[p|)`. In particular, the relative sign of its angle and square components belongs to the conversion convention and should be kept when checking a result.

For massless Dirac external fermions, give their helicities through the converter's `"FermionHelicities"` option. Its helicity values are `-1/2` and `+1/2`; this convention differs from the doubled spin labels used by exported SPINAS C++ functions.

examples.description: Use an all-incoming antifermion at the left endpoint of a scalar bilinear.

name: FermionKet
summary: Records the right fermion wavefunction of an all-incoming Dirac chain.

syntaxes.description: represents the right fermion endpoint of an ordered Dirac chain.

details: `FermionKet[leg,mass,chirality]` is the right endpoint of a [DiracChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracChain). The external-leg label and mass have the same meaning as in [FermionBar](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FermionBar).

For a massive Dirac field, use the tag `"Dirac"`. The resulting spinor expression retains the external massive spin index. The tags `"L"` and `"R"` select model field components rather than a numerical massive spin projection.
[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) uses `u = (-|p>,|p])` for this all-incoming endpoint. Its relative component sign is therefore fixed by HEPCAT's conventions.

A massless endpoint with tag `"Dirac"` needs a helicity assignment before conversion. Supply a rule such as `1 -> -1/2` through `"FermionHelicities"`. This option uses physical half-integer helicities.

examples.description: Place a momentum slash between the two external fermion wavefunctions.

name: DiracChain
summary: Represents a fermion-line numerator between specified external fermion endpoints.

syntaxes.description: joins FermionBar and FermionKet endpoints through one DiracWord.

details: `DiracChain[bar,word,ket]` joins a [FermionBar](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FermionBar) to a [FermionKet](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FermionKet) through an ordered [DiracWord](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/DiracWord). It is the Feynman representation of a fermion bilinear before conversion to angle and square brackets.

The endpoints determine the external particles and the word determines the numerator operators. A scalar coupling uses an empty word; a vector interaction inserts a gamma matrix; a fermion propagator can contribute a momentum slash.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) converts a complete contracted expression containing one or more chains. [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes) can also accept raw diagram amplitudes together with their Feynman model and perform the conversion for you.

Keep the pairing and signs produced by diagram generation when an amplitude contains several fermion lines. Exchanging endpoints by hand can change the fermionic statistics sign. All symbolic momenta use HEPCAT's all-incoming convention.

An internal slash within the word remains off shell. The external equations of motion and the Clifford algebra are sufficient for the ordinary conversion; diagram-local constructive shell assumptions are not used.

examples.description: Construct a scalar bilinear.
examples.input: bilinear = DiracChain[FermionBar[1, m, "Dirac"], DiracWord[], FermionKet[2, m, "Dirac"]]

examples.description: Convert its endpoints into spinor products.

name: PolarizationVector
summary: Records an external vector wavefunction and its Lorentz index in a Feynman diagram.

syntaxes.description: represents an external vector wavefunction in the Feynman backend.

details: `PolarizationVector[leg,index,mass,helicity]` identifies the external momentum, the Lorentz contraction index, its mass and the massless helicity when applicable. Diagram generation normally supplies this object from the process and the model.

For a massless vector, the helicity is `+1` or `-1`. In a photon process these correspond to the names `"A.+"` and `"A.-"`. A generic massless polarization needs one of these choices before it can be converted to spinor products.

For a massive vector, use `Automatic` in the last argument. [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) then retains the two symmetric little-group slots as [VectorSpinIndex](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/VectorSpinIndex) labels, so the expression describes the vector spin tensor.

Massless wavefunctions introduce auxiliary reference spinors. Choose the same reference for a given external gauge leg throughout the full Feynman sum. [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes) does this collectively for Feynman diagrams, allowing the gauge-dependent diagram contributions to combine consistently.
Reference choices can simplify intermediate expressions, but they do not change the physical amplitude. A reference giving an identically zero denominator is rejected.

examples.description: Represent photon leg 3 with positive helicity and Lorentz index mu.

name: VectorSpinIndex
summary: Labels either of the two symmetric spinor indices describing one massive-vector state.

syntaxes.description: labels one of the two symmetric little-group slots of a massive vector.

details: `VectorSpinIndex[leg,1]` and `VectorSpinIndex[leg,2]` are the two little-group slots of one massive external vector. The first argument is the external leg; the second is the slot, either `1` or `2`.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) introduces these labels when converting a massive [PolarizationVector](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PolarizationVector). Their symmetry is the spinor representation of a spin-one state. They belong to one particle, rather than to separate particles or separate polarizations.

Keep the pair while manipulating the resulting [SpinorChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/SpinorChain) expression. Combining or identifying its slots as ordinary scalar labels can lose the vector spin information.

[WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess) combines the symmetric spinor components for each vector polarization before taking the squared modulus. It then sums the probabilities for different external polarizations. This preserves the distinction between components of one state and different states.

examples.description: Inspect the two slots belonging to the same massive vector on leg 3.

name: ColorIndex
summary: Identifies the external leg associated with a symbolic color index.

syntaxes.description: labels an external color state.

details: `ColorIndex[leg]` labels an external color slot in a raw or converted Feynman amplitude. It can appear in [ColorDelta](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorDelta), [ColorGenerator](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorGenerator) and [ColorStructure](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorStructure) tensors.
External color labels remain in the symbolic expression. Internal color indices are local dummy labels whose repeated occurrences describe contractions between vertices.

[FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) converts the Lorentz and spinor part while retaining explicit color tensors. A remaining color index does not imply that a numerical sum over external colors has already been carried out.

The complete numerical [WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess) exporter currently accepts colorless amplitudes. Resolve the required color treatment before attempting a numerical export of a colored process.

examples.description: Attach the two external color labels to a color identity tensor.

name: ColorDelta
summary: Represents a Kronecker delta connecting two symbolic color indices.

syntaxes.description: represents a contracted color Kronecker tensor.

details: `ColorDelta[i,j]` records the identity contraction between two compatible color slots. A color-singlet interaction on a quark line can carry this tensor alongside its Lorentz and spinor factor.

The arguments can be external [ColorIndex](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorIndex) labels or local internal labels generated by the diagram code. Retain their contractions when simplifying the rest of the expression.
The tensor remains symbolic during Feynman-to-spinor conversion. Its presence alone does not perform external color sums, initial-color averages or a trace over all color states.

Use the model's contraction and generator conventions when comparing a colored amplitude with another calculation. See [ColorGenerator](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorGenerator) for the ordered quark-gluon generator tensor.

examples.description: Write a color identity linking external legs 1 and 2.

name: ColorGenerator
summary: Represents a fundamental SU(3) generator with ordered quark and gluon color slots.

syntaxes.description: represents a fundamental SU(3) generator.

details: `ColorGenerator[antifundamental,fundamental,adjoint]` records the color factor at a quark-gluon interaction. The order identifies which indices belong to the conjugate quark, quark and gluon representations.
The normalization is the CalcHEP generator convention `lambda/2`. Reordering the slots is therefore a change of the color tensor, rather than a display rearrangement.

HEPCAT retains this tensor when [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts) converts the accompanying Dirac and Lorentz algebra. External slots can be labeled with [ColorIndex](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ColorIndex); internal slots are local contraction labels.

An explicit generator tensor carries color-state information. A numerical squared matrix element still requires the appropriate contractions, sums and incoming-state averages. The current complete SPINAS process exporter is restricted to colorless amplitudes.

examples.description: Retain the ordered antiquark, quark and gluon color slots of a quark-gluon vertex.

name: ColorStructure
summary: Represents the SU(3) structure constant with three ordered adjoint color indices.

syntaxes.description: represents an SU(3) structure constant.

details: `ColorStructure[a,b,c]` denotes the structure constant `f(a,b,c)` appearing in gluon self-interactions. Its arguments identify the three adjoint color slots.
The tensor is antisymmetric in its color labels. Keep the ordering and accompanying scalar coefficient supplied by the model when following a diagram or comparing conventions.
In the imported CalcHEP convention, an accompanying factor of `I` from the vertex is retained separately from the structure-constant head. Removing that coefficient would change the amplitude.

The color tensor survives [FeynmanToSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanToSpinorProducts). Conversion of its Lorentz factor does not carry out external color sums or create a complete numerical color-averaged process.

examples.description: Retain the three adjoint color slots of a gluon self-interaction.

name: FeynmanToSpinorProducts
summary: Rewrites a contracted Feynman amplitude in HEPCAT angle/square spinor notation while retaining internal virtualities.

syntaxes.description: converts a contracted Feynman tensor expression.
preserves the external mass-rule pair.
converts a list of amplitude pairs.

details: Use `FeynmanToSpinorProducts` when you have a Feynman tensor expression and want to compare it with, or simplify it using, HEPCAT's [SpinorChain](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/SpinorChain) algebra. The converter handles the external wavefunctions, ordered Dirac matrices and Lorentz contractions together.

A bare expression gives a bare spinor expression. A `{massRules, expression}` pair keeps the same mass-rule list and converts its expression. A list of pairs is converted item by item, so the diagram labels and their associated external masses remain available.

For an ordinary workflow, read a [FeynmanModel](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/FeynmanModel), generate diagrams and obtain their amplitudes, then convert those amplitudes. You can instead pass the raw amplitudes and the Feynman model to [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes), which includes conversion before its reference selection and reduction.

examples.description: Convert a scalar massive-fermion bilinear.
Generate and convert the four-point QED diagrams.
Disable the final ordinary reduction to inspect the direct angle/square representation of a numerator.

detail_sections.title: What the conversion preserves
paragraphs: All momenta remain incoming. The external convention is `u=(-|p>,|p])`, `bar v=(<p|,-[p|)` and `gamma5=diag(-1,+1)`. These conventions fix the component signs in the result.

Internal Feynman momenta and propagators remain off shell. Ordinary gamma-matrix identities, Lorentz contractions and external equations of motion are applied; the converter does not set an internal momentum square to its propagator mass.

Massive external spin labels remain in the resulting spinors. A massive vector retains two symmetric [VectorSpinIndex](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/VectorSpinIndex) labels. Explicit color tensors are also retained, so conversion by itself is not a color or spin sum.

detail_sections.title: Helicities and reference spinors
paragraphs: For a massless Dirac external fermion, use `"FermionHelicities" -> {leg -> -1/2, ...}` or the corresponding positive half-integer helicity. The values are physical helicities, rather than the doubled integer labels used by exported C++ routines. Massive fermions retain their spin indices without this selection.

`"ReferenceSpinors" -> Automatic` leaves an independent auxiliary Xi spinor for each massless-vector leg. Supply rules such as `{3 -> 4, 4 -> 3}` to use other massless external legs as references; the chosen reference must give a nonzero denominator.

Use the same reference assignment for each external gauge leg in every diagram of a Feynman sum. Gauge cancellation is a property of the full amplitude. Independently optimizing the references of separate Feynman diagrams can spoil that comparison.

For the higher-level choices `"AllPhysical"` and `"AllSpurious"`, use the `"PolePreference"` option of [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes). The converter itself accepts `"ReferenceSpinors"`, not `"PolePreference"`.

detail_sections.title: Reduction and incomplete conversions
paragraphs: `"ReduceSpinorProducts" -> True` applies [ReduceSpinorProducts](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ReduceSpinorProducts) to the converted expression and uses the external masses recorded by its wavefunctions. Set the option to `False` when you want to inspect the direct result before that ordinary reduction.

A complete amplitude has every Lorentz index contracted exactly twice in each term. Free indices, unsupported endpoints or operators, and unsupported fields return `Failure`. These failures identify information that must be supplied or a form that the converter cannot yet handle.

`"MaxExpandedTerms"` bounds the exact Lorentz expansion and `"TimeConstraint"` bounds the conversion time. Exceeding either limit returns a diagnostic failure; the converter does not present a partial contraction as the complete amplitude.

name: WriteSPINASProcess
summary: Writes a runnable SPINAS C++ process from a spinor amplitude or a complete set of its helicity amplitudes.

syntaxes.description: exports one all-incoming amplitude at its fixed massless helicities.
combines helicity-related {particles, amplitude} entries into one class.
declares the physical process and crosses its outgoing legs automatically.

details: `WriteSPINASProcess` takes an amplitude that you have already obtained and writes a C++ project for evaluating it numerically with SPINAS. The default `"CodeStyle" -> "Optimized"` organizes numerical work for reuse. Select `"CodeStyle" -> "Readable"` when you want to follow the original formulas in the source. Both projects include the same process interface, example program, build instructions and manifest.

The usual input is `incoming -> outgoing`, a list of `{{particles, amplitude}, ...}` entries, and the HEPCAT model. This form states the physical reaction explicitly and lets the exporter combine its helicity sectors. Each entry still uses HEPCAT's all-incoming particle ordering and formula.
The ordinary return value is the output directory. Use `"ReturnDetails" -> True` to obtain the generated file paths, normalization information, build results and any requested validation reports.

The exporter translates the supplied amplitude; it does not derive missing contributions to it. Obtain and check the amplitude with [ConstructAmplitude](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ConstructAmplitude) or [CheckAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/CheckAmplitudes) before using it in a simulation.

examples.description: Inspect the available export options without writing files.
Export a complete four-point photon-helicity family to a temporary directory.
Optionally build the exported project and run its example points.
examples.input: WriteSPINASProcess[exportDirectory, {"e", "E"} -> {"A", "A"}, entries, knownModel, "ProcessName" -> "eeAA", "Overwrite" -> True, "Build" -> True, "RunExamples" -> True]

examples.description: Generate the independent per-helicity MadGraph report while exporting. Set the directory and model to your chosen installation and theory; this example explicitly selects the electron/positron/photon sector of sm-full.
examples.input:
madGraphDirectory = FileNameJoin[{ParentDirectory[hepcatDirectory], "MadGraph"}];
WriteSPINASProcess[exportDirectory, {"e", "E"} -> {"A", "A"}, entries, knownModel, "ProcessName" -> "eeAA", "Overwrite" -> True, "MadGraphDirectory" -> madGraphDirectory, "MadGraphModel" -> "sm-full", "MadGraphAllowedParticles" -> {11, 22}, "RunMadGraphValidation" -> True]

examples.description: Select the CalcHEP installation, model and QED sector explicitly for an independent unpolarized comparison. Replace the installation path, model directory and model number with your chosen reference.
examples.input:
calcHEPDirectory = "/path/to/CalcHEP";
WriteSPINASProcess[exportDirectory, {"e", "E"} -> {"A", "A"}, entries, knownModel, "ProcessName" -> "eeAA", "Overwrite" -> True, "CalcHEPDirectory" -> calcHEPDirectory, "CalcHEPModel" -> {feynmanModelDirectory, 2}, "CalcHEPAllowedParticles" -> {11, 22}, "RunCalcHEPValidation" -> True]

examples.description: Export the numerical MadEvent bridge and the independent validator together. Set the installation and model explicitly; this example selects only electrons, positrons and photons.
examples.input:
madGraphDirectory = FileNameJoin[{ParentDirectory[hepcatDirectory], "MadGraph"}];
WriteSPINASProcess[exportDirectory, {"e", "E"} -> {"A", "A"}, entries, knownModel, "ProcessName" -> "eeAA", "Overwrite" -> True, "Build" -> True, "MadGraphDirectory" -> madGraphDirectory, "MadGraphModel" -> "sm-full", "MadGraphAllowedParticles" -> {11, 22}]

examples.description: Use the same complete amplitude entries to request formula-oriented readable C++ instead of the optimized default. This writes a separate project.

examples.section: Reuse conjugate helicities in the spin sum
examples.description: For the tree-level vector-coupling QED family above, explicitly declare its known helicity-conjugation symmetry. Every complex helicity amplitude is still exported. The shortcut affects only the summed or averaged result.

detail_sections.title: Choose optimized or readable numerical code
paragraphs: The default `"CodeStyle" -> "Optimized"` is a numerical code-generation backend. It analyzes the expressions you supply and tracks which calculations depend on model parameters, momenta or spin labels. It uses no process-name templates, known QED answers, additional on-shell substitutions or amplitude fitting. [ConstructAmplitude](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ConstructAmplitude) and [PrepareAmplitudes](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PrepareAmplitudes) remain the tools for changing a symbolic amplitude.

The optimized native layout precomputes the spin components of supported SPINAS products into direct-access tables. Shared arithmetic that is independent of spin can be computed once per momentum point; repeated spin-dependent arithmetic stays in its proper amplitude or projection scope. Real arithmetic is used only where the form and validated inputs establish reality. Genuine complex parameters, widths and branch-sensitive operations retain their complex semantics.

Select `"CodeStyle" -> "Readable"` for the direct helicity formulas with familiar parameter, spinor-product and denominator names. This mode retains the existing numerical-constant and model-factor caches. The difference between modes is how a supplied expression is evaluated, not which amplitude is exported.

The generated class keeps the same `set_parameters`, `set_momenta`, `amp`, `spin_sum` and `amp2` conventions in both modes. Parameter updates invalidate old kinematics, and copies rebuild their own caches. Generated single-configuration builds default to Release; an explicit CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE choice is respected. No fast-math option is enabled. Floating-point grouping can affect last-bit rounding, so compare numerical tolerances rather than requiring identical bits.

The manifest and detailed result record `CodeStyle` as `Optimized` or `Readable`. `CodeLayout` separately identifies native or canonical dispatch. The `Optimization` entry records applied work sharing and unsupported or bounded fallback cases. A difficult structure keeps its supported evaluator when an optimization cannot be established; do not interpret the mode name as a promise of the fastest possible code for every process.
Reload HEPCAT and export a project again to apply a new generation mode. Recompiling C++ files that were generated earlier does not rerun the exporter.

detail_sections.title: Choosing the process and helicity coverage
paragraphs: The concatenated incoming and outgoing lists fix the numbered leg order. A physical `e,A -> e,A` process therefore has an all-incoming amplitude entry with species `e,A,E,A`. The exporter reverses the outgoing momenta and angle-spinor signs once. Supply the original all-incoming expression, without crossing it in advance.

A generic massless name such as `"A"` asks for both photon helicities. Include an amplitude for each requested sector. The exporter reuses equivalent same-role permutations of identical particles, with their statistics signs, and refuses incomplete coverage instead of inventing a missing parity-related formula.

Use `"A.+"`, `"A.-"` or `"FixedHelicities" -> {leg -> doubledHelicity}` when you want a selected incoming or outgoing massless helicity. For photons the doubled labels are `+2` and `-2`. This selection produces a labeled helicity contribution.

The four-argument `particles, amplitude, model` form exports a single fixed-helicity expression and retains its earlier normalization convention. The grouped physical-process form is the clearer choice for a complete unpolarized reaction.

detail_sections.title: What the generated numerical functions calculate
paragraphs: `amp(ds1,...,dsn)` returns the complex amplitude for one external spin/helicity assignment. Its phase is retained, and this call performs no spin sum. The generated C++ class also accepts the corresponding spin array.

`spin_sum()` evaluates the requested external states and adds `|amp|^2` for each one. It squares each state before summing: amplitudes for different external spins or helicities are not added coherently.

For a helicity family, `amp2()` also averages over unfixed incoming states and includes the final identical-species factorials once. For an unpolarized electron/positron pair producing two identical photons, these factors give `(1/8) Sum[|amp|^2]`: an initial `1/4` spin average and a final `1/2!` symmetry factor.

Fixing an incoming massless helicity removes its averaging factor. A selected outgoing helicity remains a partial contribution with the same full identical-species factorial convention. The manifest records the selection and normalization.

The symmetric spinor components describing one massive vector state are combined before squaring that state. Separate external vector polarizations are then summed as probabilities. The exported complex amplitudes retain the information needed for explicit spin-state calculations; a production-decay sewing engine is not supplied.

detail_sections.title: Reuse opposite helicities without losing polarized amplitudes
paragraphs: A complete helicity family can sometimes be evaluated with less work. In tree-level QED with real vector couplings, reversing every photon helicity gives the same squared result after summing the fermion spins. For example, `++-` and `--+` form a pair. The summed evaluator may calculate one member and count it twice. Incoming averages and identical-particle factors keep their existing values.

`"HelicitySymmetry" -> Automatic` makes a bounded exact algebraic attempt to establish this relation between the formulas that you supplied. An unproved relation keeps the exhaustive evaluator. This is a conservative optimization: a numerical agreement at a few points, a real numerical default or a particle spin does not establish the symmetry.

Use `"HelicitySymmetry" -> "Conjugation"` when you know that the complete requested spin sum has this symmetry, as for the real-coupling tree-level vector QED example above. This setting is your physical assertion, not a test of an arbitrary theory. Do not use it for unrelated weak or parity-violating interactions without establishing their relation. `"HelicitySymmetry" -> None` always retains exhaustive summation.

Pairing reverses all selected massless helicities simultaneously at the same momenta. Merely rearranging plus and minus labels is different: identical-particle exchange must also exchange the corresponding momenta. Only partners present in the requested coverage can be paired. A fixed or otherwise unpaired selection remains exhaustive; missing helicity amplitudes are never invented.

Every individual complex `amp(...)` branch and the full `helicity_configurations()` inventory remain available. This preserves polarized amplitudes and their phases for spin correlations. The shortcut is used only inside `spin_sum()` and therefore `amp2()`, where all massive external spins are summed. Both `"Readable"` and `"Optimized"` code styles support it.

The generated shortcut checks that all current parameter values are exactly real. A complex parameter update uses the exhaustive sum for those values; it is not rounded to a real value to keep the shortcut active. Nonzero or symbolic propagator widths disable pairing. This guard does not prove a user-declared symmetry between independent real couplings.

Inspect `HelicitySummation` in the manifest or detailed export result to see the paired assignments, independent evaluation count and proof or declaration mode. Fewer amplitude evaluations do not guarantee a factor-of-two speedup: momentum setup and shared numerical tables still take time.

detail_sections.title: Writing, building and changing model parameters
paragraphs: By default the exporter writes source only. `"Build" -> True` configures CMake and links the selected SPINAS library. `"RunExamples" -> True` also runs three conserved physical phase-space points. Those examples check that the generated numerical process runs; they do not compare with an independent amplitude.

`"SPINASDirectory"` selects the SPINAS installation or checkout. `"CMakeExecutable"` accepts a full CMake path when automatic discovery is unsuitable. SPINAS precision must match the library ABI; `"Precision" -> Automatic` reads the selected build configuration. HEPCAT does not install or rebuild the external library.

Numerical defaults come from the supplied model through [ModelParameterRules](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ModelParameterRules). `"ParameterRules"` overrides them for this export without assigning global values to the model's parameters. The generated mass and parameter interfaces update the process consistently when numerical values change.
`"Overwrite" -> True` permits replacing generated project files in an existing export directory. Keep saved calculations or hand-edited C++ files separately if you want to preserve them.

Current complete exports are colorless tree processes with two incoming particles and at least two outgoing particles. Resolve auxiliary Xi spinors, hats, explicit color tensors and unsupported functions before export. Unsupported input returns `Failure` rather than a partly usable numerical process.

detail_sections.title: Independent validation with CalcHEP or MadGraph
paragraphs: Independent validation compares the exported numerical expression with a separately generated reference amplitude at the same physical phase-space points. [ValidateMadGraph](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ValidateMadGraph) is the Mathematica entry point for a per-massless-helicity MadGraph comparison. A common overall amplitude phase is harmless because the comparisons use squared amplitudes.

For CalcHEP, supply `"CalcHEPDirectory"` and `"CalcHEPModel" -> {directory, modelNumber}`. `"RunCalcHEPValidation" -> True` builds and runs the independent unpolarized comparison. Fixed-helicity subsets cannot be compared with an unpolarized CalcHEP result.
For MadGraph, supply `"MadGraphDirectory"` and `"MadGraphModel"`. `"RunMadGraphValidation" -> True` checks each requested massless-helicity sector while summing massive spins in each library's basis.

Each reference generator must use the intended theory. The particle filters default to `All`; an explicit `"CalcHEPAllowedParticles" -> {11,22}` or `"MadGraphAllowedParticles" -> {11,22}` selects electrons, positrons and photons for a pure-QED comparison. Selecting the full Standard Model would also allow its other exchanges.

Used masses, couplings and width prescriptions must agree on both sides. Parameter maps relate different names, and explicit reference parameter rules resolve numerical inputs when needed. Inspect the detailed reference report if matching is ambiguous.

Automatic seeds are chosen when validation runs and are reported for replay. Requested mismatches, unavailable checks and evaluation errors return `Failure`; completing a source export or a C++ build is not reported as a successful independent validation.

detail_sections.title: Running CalcHEP integration with the HEPCAT amplitude
paragraphs: The numerical `n_calchep` backend uses CalcHEP's phase-space integration, menus, cuts, histograms and VEGAS with the supplied SPINAS matrix element. It does not ask CalcHEP to generate a symbolic reference amplitude, so an equivalent `CalcHEPModel` is not required for this numerical backend.

When the CalcHEP numerical libraries are available, the build links the executable directly at `build/results/n_calchep`, without a second copy in the build root. From the build directory, enter `results` and run `./n_calchep`. The directory belongs to the CMake build tree even when you configure an alternative build location.

The numerical parameter and mass menus are connected to the generated process, including dependent parameter functions. The explicit width prescription of the supplied amplitude is retained. Unsupported automatic-width or gauge-restoring operations are reported.

The `results` directory contains the numerical session's executable, settings and output. Move the complete directory elsewhere before deleting the enclosing build tree if you want to keep it. Installed CalcHEP and system runtime libraries remain required.

detail_sections.title: Running MadEvent integration with the HEPCAT amplitude
paragraphs: The MadEvent backend uses the explicitly selected MadGraph model to obtain particle information, parameters and phase-space topologies. Its numerical matrix element is the supplied HEPCAT/SPINAS amplitude. Independent MadGraph validation remains a separate calculation using MadGraph's own amplitude.

For a process named `eeAA`, a normal build prepares the movable `build/PROC_eeAA` numerical process. Its native `bin/madevent` is the only runtime launcher; no duplicate `eeAA_madevent` executable is created in the build root. This compiles MadEvent with the exported HEPCAT/SPINAS amplitude but does not generate events. Enter `build/PROC_eeAA` and run `./bin/madevent` for the native menu.

CMake calls the Python builder directly and keeps the numerical process in its build directory, including a custom build location. The build prints the card, HTML and event locations. Validation and example executables stay in the build root.

After preparation, enter `PROC_eeAA` and run `./bin/madevent`. Its `Cards/run_card.dat` controls beams, cuts and event settings; `Cards/param_card.dat` controls model inputs. The HTML entry page is `index.html`, and generated events are under `Events/run_name`.

The complete prepared `PROC_eeAA` directory contains its HEPCAT/SPINAS amplitude sources, headers, numerical libraries and private model support. Move that whole directory between runs if you want to keep it outside build. It then runs without the original export, build tree or SPINAS checkout. MadGraph, Python, a compatible Fortran toolchain and system libraries remain external requirements.

Repeated builds reuse the prepared process and retain its cards and events. An explicit CMake setting `-DHEPCAT_PREPARE_MADEVENT=OFF` skips automatic preparation for a C++-only build; `cmake --build build --target eeAA_madevent_process` can prepare it later. An incompatible existing session is reported rather than overwritten.

Current support is colorless leading-order tree simulation. Fixed massless helicities are retained, massive spins are summed, and incoming averages and final identical-particle factors are applied once. NLO matching, massive polarized beams, MadSpin and coherent production-decay correlations require additional interfaces and are not supplied by this bridge.

detail_sections.title: Reusing constants and parameter factors
paragraphs: Generated code separates quantities by when they can change. Fixed numerical factors, including algebraic constants such as Sqrt[2], are stored as const values and initialized once. Supported products, powers and other factors that depend only on model parameters are cached when set_parameters is called, rather than recalculated for each spin and helicity. These changes preserve the supplied formula and its complex branches; they do not apply additional spinor identities or internal on-shell conditions.

Changing masses or couplings refreshes the parameter caches and invalidates the momentum state. Copies and assignments rebuild caches against their own parameters and particles. Call set_momenta again after changing parameters. Momentum-dependent and spin-dependent values stay on their existing update paths, so an optimization cannot accidentally reuse a value from another phase-space point.

The numerical speed of a compact symbolic formula also depends on repeated divisions, shared intermediate expressions and generated function calls. Spinor products already cache their contractions. Repeated calls to the same product therefore often repeat cache access, rather than the full contraction. The benchmark described below measures the complete generated evaluation, including these costs.

detail_sections.title: Measuring numerical evaluation speed
paragraphs: The repository includes a separate C++ timing program in `benchmarks/`. It compares complete exported electron-positron to photon helicity families with independent CalcHEP and MadGraph matrix elements on the same saved phase-space points. See `benchmarks/README.md` for the build and run commands. Configure both reference models and their explicit electron/photon restrictions in [WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess) before running it.

The default measurement uses 10,000 common RAMBO points at each available photon count, full spin and helicity sums, optimized private reference builds and repeated serial timing sweeps. The CSV output contains elapsed times and three curves normalized to the two-photon case. Setup, compilation, point generation and correctness checks are excluded from the timers. An incomplete helicity family or a numerical disagreement is rejected rather than included in a performance comparison.

This benchmark measures numerical amplitude evaluation, not cross-section integration or event generation. Its MadGraph reference uses an exhaustive standalone helicity sum, not the HEPCAT matrix installed into MadEvent. Scalar precision, parameters, compiler settings, source hashes and random seed are saved so timing claims can be interpreted and repeated.

name: ValidateMadGraph
summary: Checks a HEPCAT/SPINAS amplitude against an independently generated MadGraph result at common random physical momenta.

syntaxes.description: builds and runs the MadGraph validator of a SPINAS project exported by the current WriteSPINASProcess.
exports and validates the supplied all-incoming amplitude entries for the declared physical process.
validates one all-incoming amplitude at its specified massless helicities, with IncomingLegs selecting the physical incoming pair.
returns the full report, including per-helicity failures and the actual random seed.

details: Use `ValidateMadGraph` after deriving an amplitude when you want an independent numerical check of the formula and its C++ translation. MadGraph generates its own reference matrix element; the validator evaluates both results at exactly the same physical momenta with matched parameters.

The normal result is a table with one row for each exported massless-helicity combination. A process without massless helicities has one corresponding row. A `PASS` means that all requested comparisons in that row met the stated numerical tolerance.

`ValidateMadGraph[directory]` uses an existing project written by [WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess). The amplitude-and-model forms first make a private export, build the numerical code and run the comparison. Only the comparison executable and its dependencies are built for validation, so preparing an optional MadEvent integration is a separate operation.
The comparison is a numerical test over sampled phase space. It provides an independent diagnostic of a proposed expression, rather than a proof of equality for every kinematic point.

examples.description: Inspect the validation options without running external software.

Choose a MadGraph installation and explicitly select its QED sector, then validate the complete photon-helicity family. Replace this example sibling directory and model selection with your chosen installation and theory.
Replay a run and retain its full diagnostics.
Validate a project already written by the current exporter.
Validate one amplitude with both photon helicities fixed.

detail_sections.title: Providing the reaction and the reference theory
paragraphs: Use the same `incoming -> outgoing`, helicity entries and model as for [WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess). Keep each formula all incoming; the exporter performs the outgoing momentum and spinor crossing. The four-argument fixed-helicity form retains its single-amplitude convention.

Supply `"MadGraphDirectory"` and `"MadGraphModel"` explicitly. The model can be a UFO name or directory. Choose a theory with the interactions you intend to compare; the external particle names alone do not determine which internal exchanges belong in it.

For example, `"MadGraphModel" -> "sm-full"` with `"MadGraphAllowedParticles" -> {11,22}` explicitly restricts the reference to electrons, positrons and photons. This gives a pure-QED comparison while retaining the model's massive electron. Leaving the particle filter at `All` allows every interaction of the selected model, including its Z and Higgs exchanges when relevant.

Particle filters use positive absolute PDG codes, include their antiparticles and must contain every external particle type. Unsupported or inconsistent selections produce a diagnostic instead of a passing comparison.

detail_sections.title: Helicities, spin sums and phases
paragraphs: The validator checks each requested massless-helicity assignment separately. The table displays labels such as `3:-, 4:+`; details retain the original leg-order vectors with doubled integer helicities, such as `-2` and `+2` for photons.
Massive spins are summed on each side. Individual massive spin components can use different bases in MadGraph and SPINAS, so their complex numbers are not compared component by component.

Each comparison uses a squared amplitude. An overall phase, including a sign or a factor of `I`, therefore does not cause a mismatch. Relative phases between contributions to the same amplitude remain essential because they affect interference.

Incoming averages and outgoing identical-species factors are matched once. A fixed incoming or outgoing massless helicity remains the selected contribution; it is not silently replaced by an unpolarized sum.

detail_sections.title: Sampling and understanding a failed comparison
paragraphs: `"MadGraphPoints" -> 1000` requests 1000 common physical points for every massless-helicity combination. `"MadGraphSeed" -> Automatic` selects a seed at run time and reports it. Supply an unsigned 64-bit integer, including zero, to repeat a particular sample sequence.

`"RelativeTolerance" -> 10^-7` and `"AbsoluteTolerance" -> 0` are the default numerical tolerances. Nonfinite values, missing evaluations and runtime errors cannot count as a pass. The full report retains the first failing momenta and the concrete seed.

Use `"MinimumEnergy"` and `"MaximumEnergy"` to restrict the sampled center-of-mass energies. Automatic choices lie above the process thresholds. These random points are validation probes, rather than an integration result or a cross section.

A failure can expose numerical conditioning as well as an incorrect expression. At high energy, large cancellations or inverse small masses can make one form lose precision even when a more compact equivalent form is stable. Compare the failed values and momenta before loosening a tolerance.

detail_sections.title: Matching parameters and widths
paragraphs: The HEPCAT model supplies its numerical inputs through [ModelParameterRules](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/ModelParameterRules). `"MadGraphParameterMap" -> {"HEPCATName" -> "UFOName", ...}` relates differently named parameters; `"MadGraphParameterRules"` supplies explicit external UFO input values when necessary.

A name mapping does not by itself change a derived UFO coupling to an arbitrary value. Its value must agree with the selected model's independent inputs. Ambiguous or inconsistent matching produces a diagnostic before the comparison can pass.

The two sides must also use the same propagator-width prescription. A bare [PropDen](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/PropDen) has no decay width, so independently adjustable, unmatched MadGraph decay-width inputs are set to zero. Explicit reference width rules and matched width parameters retain their supplied values. The detailed reference report records this choice.

detail_sections.title: Reports and external software
paragraphs: `"Output" -> "Summary"` gives status counts. `"Output" -> "Details"` gives the complete report, including reference setup, helicity selection, numerical errors and failed momenta. These reports help distinguish a theory mismatch from a sampling or numerical problem.

The current validator supports colorless tree processes with two incoming particles, at least two outgoing particles and external spins through one. It requires MadGraph, a Fortran compiler, SPINAS and the normal C++ build tools. Ordinary source-only SPINAS exports remain available without those reference tools.
`"TimeConstraint" -> 600` bounds MadGraph reference preparation. It does not impose a single deadline on the complete CMake build and all requested numerical samples.

The directory form uses the process, model, parameter matching and fixed-helicity selection saved in that export. You can vary sampling controls such as points, seed, tolerances and energy bounds. To change the stored reaction or reference theory, regenerate the project or use an amplitude-and-model form.

For numerical event generation with the HEPCAT amplitude, use the MadEvent launcher generated by [WriteSPINASProcess](paclet:HEPCAT/ref/WriteSPINASProcess). Running that simulation does not replace the independent comparison provided by `ValidateMadGraph`.
